title: When the Atlas Wakes
premise: In the winter of 1899, Beatrix Crane tends the lighthouse at Greyhollow Point and keeps her late husband's secret ledger of the town's debts and debts forgiven. When the army requisitions the coastal town to build storm defenses, Captain Elias Vane demands the ledger as evidence of sedition among the fishermen, forcing Beatrix to choose between the truth it holds and the neighbors it could destroy. As the great storms close in, she allies with Tomas Reyes, a conscripted cartographer who once loved her, to forge a second ledger that will hang the guilt on the dead quartermaster who caused it all. The workshop burns on the last night of the century; Beatrix surrenders the false ledger, keeps the true one buried beneath the lighthouse, and chooses neither man nor duty but the light itself.
about_author: Petra Eriksen is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse keepers' logs along the North Atlantic coast. Her novels are known for their salt-bleached prose and their insistence that ordinary record-keepers are the quiet engines of history.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. On a calm October morning, Beatrix trims the wicks, mends nets, and opens her husband's ledger to record a widow's forgiven debt. The emotional beat is quiet grief transformed into purpose: the ledger is her marriage's afterlife, and she guards it like a second flame.

chapters.title: Grey Boats, Grey Water
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The fishing fleet returns short one boat and two men; Beatrix records their debts as forgiven and lies to the widow about how they died. She begins to understand the ledger's power — and its danger. The beat is the first crack between mercy and truth.

chapters.title: Soldiers at the Harbor
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The army arrives by steamer to requisition Greyhollow for storm defenses, and cartographer Tomas Reyes recognizes the lighthouse — and the woman in it — from a life he abandoned. His beat is dread braided with longing as he signs the requisition order.

chapters.title: The Captain's Questions
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Captain Vane quarters himself in the town hall and announces that sedition is spreading among the fishermen; he requires all records of debt, allegiance, and correspondence. Beatrix hides the ledger in the lighthouse's oil store. The beat is cold fear managed by busy hands.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Holds
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, with flashbacks to her husband Aldous. We learn the ledger records not only debts but the smuggling ring that kept the town alive through famine years — and that Aldous died protecting it. The beat is a deepening of stakes: the book is a noose for half the town.

chapters.title: A Map of Small Treasons
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Vane orders Tomas to survey the coast and mark every household 'loyal' or 'suspect.' Tomas fudges his first marks to protect a fisherman's family and realizes he is already a traitor. The beat is the intoxication and terror of small disobedience.

chapters.title: Oil and Salt
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Tomas's alternating POV. Tomas comes to the lighthouse under survey pretext; they circle each other over tea and ten years of silence. She neither forgives nor dismisses him. The beat is wary tenderness, two people measuring old wounds by lamplight.

chapters.title: The Quartermaster's Ghost
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas discovers the army's own quartermaster, Hobb, has been selling requisitioned supplies back to the townsfolk at famine prices — the very 'sedition' Vane hunts. Hobb is the true author of the town's desperation. The beat is righteous anger with nowhere lawful to go.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Soldiers occupy the lighthouse's lower gallery and convert the workshop to a signal station; Beatrix is ordered to keep the light burning for military convoys only. The beat is violation — her sanctuary conscripted, her purpose redirected.

chapters.title: The Storm That Took His Boat
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The first great storm hits; Beatrix defies orders and sweeps the light toward the fishing fleet, saving eleven boats. Vane witnesses the disobedience and says nothing — yet. The beat is defiant love, the keeper's duty to people over orders.

chapters.title: Confession by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas tells Beatrix about Hobb and proposes the forgery: a second ledger implicating Hobb in the smuggling ring, dated and aged, to be 'discovered' in the dead man's effects. The beat is the dangerous thrill of a plan that could save or hang them both.

chapters.title: The Workshop at Night
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix begins the forgery in the workshop below the light, copying Aldous's hand — a hand she knows better than her own. Tomas forges the survey seals. The beat is intimate complicity; love arriving disguised as conspiracy.

chapters.title: Vane's Mercy
chapters.summary: Vane's POV, the book's only chapter in the antagonist's head. Vane, himself a keeper's son, interrogates a boy and hates what he's become. He suspects the ledger exists and that Beatrix holds it. The beat is the antagonist humanized — duty as a kind of drowning.

chapters.title: The Widow's Testimony
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. A widow, pressured by Vane, nearly reveals the debt-forgiveness entries. Beatrix lies under oath at the town hall to protect her. The beat is the cost of loyalty: Beatrix becomes, for the first time, a liar in a room of lawful men.

chapters.title: Hobb's Price
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Hobb discovers Tomas's doctored survey marks and blackmails him: help him flee with the army's pay chest, or be exposed. Tomas agrees, secretly planning to use the escape to plant the forged ledger in Hobb's baggage. The beat is a gambler's calm over panic.

chapters.title: The Second Great Storm
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The worst storm in a generation batters the point; the military light fails, and Beatrix restores the civilian lamp by hand, burned and half-blind, guiding both fleet and gunboats to safety. The beat is transcendence through endurance — the light as moral act.

chapters.title: What Vane Saw
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane, watching the light burn against his orders, understands Beatrix's character completely — and decides she is either the town's traitor or its conscience. He orders a search of the lighthouse at dawn. The beat is the noose tightening with grudging respect.

chapters.title: The Buried Book
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Before dawn, Beatrix seals the true ledger in an oilskin and iron box and buries it beneath the lighthouse foundation stone, keeping only the forgery. The beat is a quiet funeral for truth-as-evidence; some truths must outlive the law to survive it.

chapters.title: Discovery
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Vane's search finds nothing at the lighthouse, but Hobb's flight is exposed; in his seized baggage, soldiers find the forged ledger. Hobb, cornered, names Tomas. Vane must choose whom to believe. The beat is the trap springing — on the right man, by the wrong means.

chapters.title: The Burning of the Workshop
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Tomas's alternating POV. On the last night of 1899, Hobb, escaping, fires the workshop; Beatrix and Tomas save the light mechanism but lose the forge, the seals, and nearly their lives. Vane arrives to arrest them and instead fights the fire beside them. The beat is the climax's moral pivot: shared danger dissolving the law's claim.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At midnight, bells and foghorns mark the new century. Vane, holding the forged ledger and knowing in his bones it is false, closes his inquiry: Hobb is blamed, the town spared, and he requests transfer rather than live with what he knows. The beat is exhausted, imperfect justice — mercy wearing the law's uniform.

chapters.title: The Light Keeps Itself
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, final chapter. In spring, the army withdraws; Tomas chooses to stay and rebuild the workshop, and Beatrix lets him — not as a replacement for grief but as a companion to it. She digs up the true ledger, adds one new name in her own hand, and buries it again. The beat is resolution: the truth kept, not told; the light lit, night after night, for no one and everyone.
